claim: Illusory inferences are systematic: confident, uniform errors on problems where reasoning from true cases only gives a wrong answer. Found with propositional, embedded-disjunction, quantified, modal and conditional problems. Human rates from originals: modal 15% correct vs 91% on controls (N=20), embedded disjunctions 19% vs 95%, conditionals 6% vs 83% (N=80, Spanish lab, r=.87, only partly independent of the Johnson-Laird network). Illusions of impossibility are weaker than illusions of possibility (quantified problems, Yang & Johnson-Laird: 67% vs 23% correct; 54% pooled over both kinds). LLMs also produce the predicted fallacies on disjunction problems (d01, d02), though those tests are by a rival theory's authors and have no matched controls. Gap pass: an independent lab (Sable-Meyer & Mascarenhas 2021, N=64 and 70 analysed) found the disjunction illusion again with controls at 87%/26% and 90%/20% accepted, and showed it is triggered by knowledge links, not only word overlap (d24).
agent_test: Build a code-generated set of illusion items and matched controls on the same premises (different question). Run the plain model at equal tokens, 20+ items per type, and report illusion vs control accuracy.
audit_note: The 'about 54% pooled correct' is Yang & Johnson-Laird Exp 1 correct rate over ALL quantified illusions (possibility 23%, impossibility 67%), not illusions of impossibility alone; other numbers (15/91 N=20, 19/95, 6/83 N=80 r=.87) check out.
claim_before_audit: Illusory inferences are systematic: confident, uniform errors on problems where reasoning from true cases only gives a wrong answer. Found with propositional, embedded-disjunction, quantified, modal and conditional problems. Human rates from originals: modal 15% correct vs 91% on controls (N=20), embedded disjunctions 19% vs 95%, conditionals 6% vs 83% (N=80, Spanish lab, r=.87, only partly independent of the Johnson-Laird network). Illusions of impossibility are weaker (about 54% pooled correct). LLMs also produce the predicted fallacies on disjunction problems (d01, d02), though those tests are by a rival theory's authors and have no matched controls. Gap pass: an independent lab (Sable-Meyer & Mascarenhas 2021, N=64 and 70 analysed) found the disjunction illusion again with controls at 87%/26% and 90%/20% accepted, and showed it is triggered by knowledge links, not only word overlap (d24).

claim: Confidence does not separate right from wrong on illusions: 4.4 vs 4.3 of 5 (Johnson-Laird & Savary 1999 Exp 1), 4.17 vs 4.24 (Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird 2000 Exp 3), 3.9 vs 4.0 of 5 (Espino et al. 2024, N=80), 5.45 to 6.26 of 7 with no reliable differences (Khemlani & Johnson-Laird 2009). A reasoner's own confidence cannot trigger doubt on this error class in humans. For LLMs this is untested: no study measured LLM confidence or sample agreement on illusion items.
agent_test: On illusion items, compare stated confidence and sample agreement for correct vs incorrect answers. If errors are uniform across fresh samples, disagreement will not flag them.
audit_note: Cited confidence values match Goldvarg and Johnson-Laird, Espino et al. and Khemlani and Johnson-Laird; JL&S 1999 not opened; note Yang and Johnson-Laird found a small reliable confidence gap (.13), and 4 of 5 sources are one lab.

claim: A generic warning ('beware, tricky') or an explicit rubric ('only one is true') does not remove illusions. A procedural check instruction (confirm one premise stays true and the other false) helps but leaves large error: illusions 30% to 71% (Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird 2000 Exp 3, N=20 in two groups), 39% to 71% (Yang & Johnson-Laird 2000 Exp 2, N=20). For GPT-4 a plain control prompt blocked as many ETR fallacies as a theory-based prose prompt (8/19 vs 7/19). Whether a code-built table beats a prose check at equal tokens is untested.
agent_test: Arms at equal tokens: plain; plain plus warning; plain plus rubric; case-split procedure. Expect the warning arm to equal plain.

claim: Forcing the reasoner to work out 'premise 1 true and 2 false' then 'premise 2 true and 1 false' closes the illusion-control gap but costs accuracy on controls and leaves about 29% error. Confirmed in the original (Yang & Johnson-Laird 2000): Exp 1 illusions 33% to 65% with controls 93% to 79% (z=2.31); Exp 2 illusions 39% to 71% with controls 87% to 72% (z=1.99, p<.05). The two groups' gap vanished (z=0.44). Same lab and small N (20 per experiment). LLM check (c08, Koralus & Wang-Masciantica 2023, re-read): an erotetic "turn each premise into questions, list alternatives" prompt blocked a previously produced fallacy on 14/17 vs 4/17 for GPT-3.5 (p=.0045) but 8/19 vs 7/19 for GPT-4 (control step-by-step 8, erotetic 7). Only items that had already failed were retested, so the effect is not separated from regression to the mean.
agent_test: Implement as an operator: for an 'only one is true' item, code lists each truth assignment and the model fills in what follows in each. Compare with plain on illusion items AND controls (cost check), equal tokens.

claim: Difficulty tracks the number of models to be held: one-model problems are much easier than multiple-model problems in syllogisms (80% vs 21%, Exp 1), set membership (92% vs 51%) and relational inference (98/72/8% for transitive/pseudotransitive/non-transitive). Boundary: for embedded disjunctions, model count alone does not explain difficulty (3-model illusions harder than 4-model controls).
agent_test: Code counts models per item. Check whether LLM accuracy falls with model count on syllogisms and set-membership items, at equal tokens. Use the count to allocate checking budget (G12). Caveat: all four sources are the same lab network, so independence is weak.
audit_note: Numbers match (80/21, 92/51, 98/72/8), but every source is a Johnson-Laird-lab paper (Bucciarelli, Khemlani, Goodwin, all co-authored by the theory's author); no outside lab replicates the model-count effect, and the relational 98/72/8 is cited from earlier work.

claim: 'Nothing follows' is a hard case for humans and a very hard one for LLMs. Humans do worse on no-valid-conclusion items (50% in Exp 1) than on one-model items (80%), though better than on multiple-model items (21%) (Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird); LLMs rarely produce it (PaLM 2, Pythia, LLaMA) and drift to form-based (atmosphere) answers; in-context examples did not fix it for the open models.
agent_test: Always add an explicit 'no valid conclusion' candidate in harvest and test it with a code counterexample search. Measure NVC-item accuracy plain vs scaffold. Models tested are 2023-24 PaLM 2 and open models up to 70B, not frontier ones.
audit_note: In Bucciarelli and Johnson-Laird, no-valid-conclusion items (50%, 41% in Exp 2) are harder than one-model items (80%) but easier than multiple-model items (21%), so it is not 'the hard case' for humans; the LLM part (rarely say 'nothing follows', ICL does not fix it) is supported by Eisape et al. and Bertolazzi et al.
claim_before_audit: 'Nothing follows' is the hard case for humans and for LLMs. Humans do worse on no-valid-conclusion items (50% vs 80% one-model in Exp 1 of Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird); LLMs rarely produce it (PaLM 2, Pythia, LLaMA) and drift to form-based (atmosphere) answers; in-context examples did not fix it for the open models. c01 is the same paper as a26/b25 (Eisape 2024), so it is not an extra source.

claim: Say: Humans and 2023-24 LLMs share some systematic syllogism errors (figural effect, top human fallacies) but differ on 'nothing follows' responses; then keep the numbers as written.
agent_test: Check whether the agent's errors on the 64 syllogisms repeat across fresh samples (same wrong answer). If yes, voting cannot fix them; counterexample search should.
audit_note: Numbers match (W .86/.64, 75% vs 50%, 58.89 vs 44.63, r=0.80 for base LLaMA-3 70B), but Eisape et al. say only that some model errors mirror human ones, and models almost never answer 'nothing follows' unlike humans, so 'the same few systematic errors' is too strong.
claim_before_audit: Humans and LLMs of 2023-24 make the same few systematic syllogism errors. Human difficulty ranking is stable across six studies (Kendall W .86 valid, .64 invalid). Larger PaLM 2 models beat humans (about 75% vs 50%) yet still show figural effects and the top human fallacies. Bertolazzi 2024 (c06, re-read): LLaMA-3 70B 58.89% on valid vs human 44.63%, correlation 0.80 with the human difficulty ordering.

claim: No single syllogism theory is adequate. The original mental-models program predicts too many conclusions (95% hits, 74% correct rejections); verbal models are best balanced (84% overall); model-based theories beat heuristic ones in aggregate (76% vs 66%). mReasoner was built to replace the deterministic program.
agent_test: Do not hard-wire one theory. Use only code-checkable parts (model enumeration, counterexample search) and test each at equal tokens.

claim: In mReasoner fits, deliberate counterexample search separates better from poorer reasoners (search propensity .4 vs .8; model size 2.0 vs 4.5; mean individual fit r .70, subgroups .78 to .91; no concordance of individual parameters, Kendall's W=.28, p=.33; set-membership search .58). All fits are in-sample with free parameters by the theory's authors. It says search separates good from poor reasoners, not what should trigger it; no study tests triggered search vs always-on search. Gap pass: no test of what should trigger search was found; d23 shows disagreement-triggered verification beats always-on on non-logic tasks only.
agent_test: Vary the search rate in the scaffold (never, on signal, always) on syllogism and set-membership items; compare accuracy and tokens. Prediction: on-signal beats always at equal tokens.

claim: Practice gain without feedback is real but possibly a response-bias shift. Small retest (N=20): 58% to 68%, 19 of 20 improved. Independent lab (N=100, full text read): session 1 overall 50.1% to session 2 52.7%; valid items 55.5% to 60.3%, invalid 46.1% to 47.2%; gain with trial number significant only for valid items in session 1; larger fall in NVC answers on multiple-model valid items; authors give two explanations (NVC aversion, or a new strategy misapplied to invalid items) and do not separate them. No LLM test found.
agent_test: Do not credit within-task adaptation without a held-out check (G3). Test whether an in-context history of earlier items changes accuracy on held-out NVC items, or only the NVC response rate.

claim: Added background content suppresses or invites conditional inferences (Byrne 1989, N=24, 3 groups of 8: modus ponens 96% simple vs 38% with an additional requirement; affirmation of the consequent 71% vs 13% with an alternative). Restating a problem can change which possibilities are in play.
agent_test: Run conditional items with and without an added requirement sentence. Check LLM modus ponens suppression and whether S1 restatement that keeps the premises verbatim preserves behaviour.

claim: People reason about possibility parsimoniously: they accept inferences invalid in modal logic K and reject valid ones. Model theory predicts 80% (Exp 1, N=53) and 83% (Exp 2, N=51) of evaluations vs 56% and 50% for logic K. Where the two disagree: Exp 1 Yes 84%, No 81%; Exp 3 (N=50) Yes 89%, No 76% in the theory's favour.
agent_test: Only matters if a task uses possibility wording. Define the norm (logic or human) for the grader first; compare LLM answers to both.

claim: Naive probability: people count equiprobable models of what is true. Judgements are biased when the stated models differ from the fully explicit ones (1.1 of 8 unbiased vs 5.6 of 9 on controls, N=25). Combining probabilities of unique events is often incoherent (56% violations, N=39). Integer-case formats rescue Bayesian-style tasks (53% vs 8%, cited second-hand).
agent_test: Compare a model-only probability answer with a code-expanded state table with counted cases on 20 problems. Also test sum-to-one normalisation over exclusive answers.
audit_note: Numbers verified (5.6 vs 1.1 unbiased, 56% violations N=39, 53% vs 8% cited second-hand from Girotto and Gonzalez), but both papers are Johnson-Laird-lab work testing his own theory; the Bayesian rescue figure is only a citation; the notes' 'r=.76' is actually R2.

claim: In Wason selection tasks people select instances of the hypothesis, its potential counterexamples, or both, depending on content and instructions (meta-analysis of 228 experiments, Ragni & Kola 2018); with feedback in the repeated selection task they switched from instances to potential counterexamples. When judging given conclusions, counterexample use was higher and correct rejection lower for conclusions merely consistent with the premises than for inconsistent ones (use 51% vs 21%; correct rejection 74% vs 92%; Johnson-Laird 2010, citing one study).
agent_test: Give the model conclusions consistent with but not entailed by the premises. Test plain vs forced counterexample search; measure false acceptance. Note a11 is second-hand inside a review and b29 was a snippet, so the 'two sources' are thin.
audit_note: 51/21 and 74/92 match Johnson-Laird 2010 (a self-review of one cited study); but the 228 experiments show people select instances, counterexamples or both (not simply 'default confirming'), and the feedback switch comes from the repeated selection task, not the 228-study meta-analysis; both sources are model-theory authors' work.
claim_before_audit: Without feedback the default is to test confirming instances; feedback shifts people toward counterexamples (228 selection-task experiments). Counterexample use is higher, and rejection worse, for conclusions merely consistent with the premises (use 51% vs 21%; rejection 74% vs 92%).

claim: A short 'model method' (list the possibilities for each premise, strike those ruled out) is reported to raise correct inferences from about 63-65% to 95% and cut time from 24-25 s to 15 s after about 2 minutes of teaching. The two reports by Johnson-Laird (2012, 2024) give different control values (65% vs 63%, 25 s vs 24 s). The source is an unpublished 1999 PhD thesis (Bell). No N, no design, no independent replication.
agent_test: Test a list-the-possibilities template vs plain at equal tokens. Treat 95% as unverified.

claim: The spin-off claim that valid conclusions feel more fluent (liked more) vanishes when conclusion content is randomised across valid and invalid; content confounds fake it.
agent_test: Randomise content across valid and invalid items in every evaluation. Do not use fluency or a self-rated sense of validity as a signal.

claim: Conditional reasoning: no single theory wins across tasks. Response patterns are more redundant than independent-choice simulations predict (39 experiments, 2378 participants), against independent-inference theories. Model-theory variants hold up only with add-ons (directionality, dual process).
agent_test: Keep the task format (produce, evaluate, choose) the same between test and deployment. Test format sensitivity on conditional items. b22 was an abstract only.

claim: A believable conclusion tends to end the search for alternative models (belief bias), and people differ in whether they look for a second model. LLMs show content effects on syllogisms: open 2024 models lose 8% to 40% on valid unbelievable items (the largest instruct model does not); 14 models in 2025 show a mean belief bias of +10.81 pp (p=.028, d=0.66), with top models under 2 pp and weak ones up to 46.9 pp (judge-validity task, not conclusion generation). Whether a counterexample search removes the effect has no test. Gap pass: in ten open models (Qwen, Gemma, 2025-26) chain of thought lowers the content effect and all exceed 89% accuracy; zero-shot content effect rises with validity-plausibility vector similarity (d22). No frontier or counterexample-vs-flag test found.
agent_test: Hold form constant and swap believable/unbelievable content; compare plain and counterexample-search arms. b29 was a search summary only, so use a10, a27 and b24 for numbers.

claim: LLMs produce human-like disjunction fallacies and capability does not remove them. Across 38 models on 383 generated fallacy-eliciting problems the mean correct rate was 40.6% (max 91.7%) with no relation to Arena Elo (r=0.004); the share of wrong answers that are the predicted fallacy rose with Elo (Spearman .36, p=.0265). Reversing premise order blocked the fallacy for 37% to 68% of fallacies in four models. GPT-3 to GPT-4: fallacy production 18% to 34%. c07 is the same paper as d02 (checked: 18%, 33%, 34% human-like fallacy output for GPT-3, 3.5, 4; ETR-predicted 59/77/75%), so it adds no independent source. Gap pass (d28): no test of current frontier or reasoning-model chat systems on the classic illusions was found; the claim rests on 2023-24 chat models and the 38-model set.
agent_test: Make 20+ illusion items with matched controls from code, run the current model plain, report both rates and a premise-reversed variant. Both tests so far are by one theory group (Oxford, ETR) and have no human rates on the same items.

claim: The size of an illusion depends on framing and answer format. Same premises: physical-object disjunctions 84% vs logical 19% correct (Santamaria & Johnson-Laird 2000); yes/no format 63% correct vs 19% in the open-choice format (Khemlani & Johnson-Laird 2009); co-reference across premises changes illusion rates (Walsh & Johnson-Laird 2004, 10% correct on illusions vs 78% on controls, N=35). Human results are therefore not one number.
agent_test: Fix the answer format (yes/no/cannot tell) and randomise referents and content in every illusion test, and report which format was used.

claim: A one-time illusion fix does not equal a general fix. A two-case procedure costs about 15 points on controls (93 to 79, 87 to 72) in Yang & Johnson-Laird 2000 and leaves 29% error on illusions. A table that always fires should be gated by a signal or shown to be cost-free on controls.
agent_test: Measure control cost when the table fires on every item vs only on a flagged subset, at equal tokens.

claim: Models seldom enumerate possibilities on their own: symbolic (truth-table) strategies are rare in open LLMs (Llama-2-70B sound reasoning in 31.7% of cases), and PaLM 2 models answer 'nothing follows' with accuracy near 0% under zero-shot CoT. An enumeration or NVC-candidate operator would add behaviour that the model does not show spontaneously.
agent_test: Check whether current frontier models enumerate when asked about illusions, and whether an explicit NVC option changes the NVC rate on the 37 NVC syllogisms.
audit_note: Mondorf and Plank (31.7% Llama-2-70B sound, symbolic strategy only occasional) and Eisape et al. (NVC accuracy near 0%) match; note Zephyr-7B uses the symbolic strategy most often among tested models, and the closing design inference is the notes' own.

claim: Fixed answer keys matter. Syllogism validity labels depend on whether existential import is assumed, and larger or reasoning models shift toward modern logic (Zang et al. 2026, abstract-level). A grader must state the convention or it will score modern-logic answers as errors.
agent_test: Set the existential-import rule in the key before scoring the 64 syllogisms and report both keys.

claim: LLM probability judgments are incoherent in human-like ways (identities broken, inverted-U mean-variance) for GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA-2 on 24 event pairs. Human naive-probability errors: JPD violated on 56% of trials (N=39). Nobody has tested whether a code-built table of full states plus counting fixes the LLM errors, or whether it beats sum-to-one normalisation.
agent_test: Items from the unique-event paradigm (P(A), P(B), P(A and B), P(A and not B)); arms plain, normalise to 1, code-built full-state table with the model filling the cells. Score JPD violations.

claim: Models fail systematically on conditional and modal inference. Nearly all the LLMs tested accepted two clearly invalid modal inferences (must(A or B) so must A or must B; might A and might B so might(A and B)). Zero-shot chain of thought added 0.2 to 21.5 points; few-shot gave -8 to +12.5. This is the same family as Johnson-Laird's possibility illusions but with logic-style items, not his materials.
agent_test: Run the two invalid modal patterns on our agent plain vs with an explicit possibility table, 20 items each, equal tokens; score acceptance of the invalid pattern.

claim: Models over-apply a rule that the premises do not license when background facts make the rule inapplicable (Rulebreakers). Models near perfect on ordinary modus tollens and disjunctive syllogism items were at 0.0022 to about 0.3 paired accuracy on rulebreakers; best of 7 models under 0.7. Logic-style chain of thought or symbolic translation raised ordinary accuracy and lowered rulebreaker accuracy. Rewording helped up to 24 points but no model passed 69%. This is the mental-models principle that knowledge can block a formal inference.
agent_test: Rulebreaker items: plain vs a 'does background knowledge block this rule?' check, scoring paired accuracy; check the check does not hurt ordinary items.

claim: Premise order and counterfactual content hurt LLM deduction. Permuting premise order can cause accuracy drops of over 30% (Chen et al. 2024; models tested include GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro). Premises that contradict world knowledge cost an average 14% across 11 models; a flag-and-reason prompt cut the gap to 7% and raised overall accuracy 4%. Note the Johnson-Laird view predicts order effects (model construction is serial) and belief effects (believable conclusions stop search), but neither paper tests it. Gap pass: no 2025-26 premise-order measurement on frontier or reasoning models for deduction was found; d26 is training-based on 7B-70B models and d27 shows order effects of 13-22% in frontier models on moral judgments only.
agent_test: Shuffle premise order and add belief-conflicting versions of 50 items; compare plain, a code-ordered restatement, and flag-and-reason at equal tokens.
audit_note: Chen et al. say permuting premise order 'can cause' a drop of over 30% (a maximum, not a drop shown for each listed model); the 14%, 7% and +4% figures (11 LLMs), and the 13-22% moral-judgment order effects match their abstracts.
claim_before_audit: Premise order and counterfactual content hurt LLM deduction. Reordering premises dropped accuracy by over 30% (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro). Premises that contradict world knowledge cost an average 14% across 11 models; a flag-and-reason prompt cut the gap to 7% and raised accuracy 4%. Note the Johnson-Laird view predicts order effects (model construction is serial) and belief effects (believable conclusions stop search), but neither paper tests it. Gap pass: no 2025-26 premise-order measurement on frontier or reasoning models for deduction was found; d26 is training-based on 7B-70B models and d27 shows order effects of 13-22% in frontier models on moral judgments only.

claim: Spatial and 'visualise the state' prompting helps on some tasks and not others. Visualization-of-Thought gave GPT-4 +23.5 (relative or points, the text says %) over no-visualisation on natural-language navigation and 87.1% vs 57.4% complete tracking in tiling, but chain of thought beat it on ring navigation (52.5 vs 49.5, N=200). Pure-text spatial benchmarks show models above 0.85 on retrieval and much lower on physical-constraint items. Spatial mental-model work in vision-language models (MindCube) finds that a self-built cognitive map helps only when generated before reasoning.
agent_test: Use an explicit coordinate state written to a scratch table for spatial items; compare against prose chain of thought at equal tokens.

claim: Spatial reasoning models fit human data only modestly above plain logic. In four datasets (33, 30, 49, 51 participants) the best model predicted 71.9% to 79.1% of answers; a transitive-closure baseline reached 73.4 to 75%. Best-of-models upper bounds were 76 to 100%. So model-theory-style spatial models add little on easy relational items.
agent_test: None needed for the scaffold; use as a warning not to build elaborate model construction for easy relational items.

claim: An external checker telling ChatGPT that its answer is wrong (no counterexample content) improved it only slowly: gpt-3.5 rose from 47.27% to 56.64% and gpt-4o from 77.39% to 80.01% on 256 syllogism satisfiability tasks over up to 10 rounds, with 111 and 51 tasks never solved (Dong et al.). Separately, in blocks-world planning GPT-4 alone solved 19/20 problems at 3 blocks and 2/20 at 10 blocks, and Jha et al. use solver counterexamples in an LLM loop, but that paper's baseline numbers here do not measure how much counterexample feedback helps.
agent_test: Counterexample feedback loop with code-checked invalidity (not a hint of the right answer) vs plain retry at equal tokens, on syllogism NVC items.
audit_note: Numbers match (Dong et al. 47.27->56.64, 77.39->80.01, 111 and 51 tasks; Jha et al. 19/20 vs 2/20), but Dong's feedback was only 'your answer is not correct' (no counterexample), and the Jha figures are GPT-4 baseline success by problem size, not a measured effect of counterexample feedback, so 'counterexample feedback helps but is weak' is not shown.
claim_before_audit: LLMs given a counterexample from a solver improve slowly: with only 'wrong' feedback gpt-3.5 rose from 47.27% to 56.64% and gpt-4o from 77.39% to 80.01% on 256 syllogism satisfiability tasks over 10 rounds, with 111 and 51 tasks never solved. In blocks-world planning, GPT-4 alone solved 19/20 problems at 3 blocks and 2/20 at 10 blocks. External counterexample feedback helps but without a model to build from it is weak.

claim: Triggered verification can beat always-on verification at lower token cost, but only for errors that vary between samples. Derailer-Rerailer (math, symbolic, commonsense) with Claude-3.5-Sonnet: 82.1% at 0.592K tokens vs 80.0% at 1.458K for always-on Rerailer and 79.8% at 1.732K for self-consistency; Rerailer fixes 9.5% of wrong answers and breaks 1.8% of right ones. Uniform errors such as illusions and syllogism mistakes (A01.01-K02, A01.01-K07) are the case a disagreement trigger misses.
agent_test: Arms at equal tokens on illusion, syllogism and control items: never verify, always verify, verify on sample disagreement, verify on a code-detected item signal (multiple-model item, only-one-true rubric, nothing-follows candidate). Report the share of errors each trigger catches.

claim: Illusions are not explained by inattention or by exact word matching alone. In an independent lab, accuracy on controls went with a steeper fall for the illusion (slope .97, R2=.9, 7 items, Exp 1), and a rating of the causal link between premises predicted acceptance of an unmatched fallacy. A competing line shows surface matching heuristics produce below-chance accuracy when matching and logic disagree (N=409, 4 experiments).
agent_test: Include illusion items with word-overlap and with knowledge-link triggers, plus items where matching and logic disagree. Check that a code-built possibility table beats plain on all three.

claim: OPEN GAP: no study was found that tests current frontier or reasoning LLMs on (a) Johnson-Laird illusions with matched controls, (b) a code-built possibility table versus plain and versus a warning, (c) an explicit nothing-follows option with counterexample search on 64 syllogisms with a fixed existential-import key, (d) a code counting table for probability beyond sum-to-one normalisation, (e) code-reordered premises. These need our own tests; outside numbers do not exist for them.
agent_test: Run in the harness as the first mental-models tests: illusion-vs-control table test (gaps 1,2), NVC option test (gap 4), counting table test (gap 9), premise-reorder test (gap 10), each at equal tokens with plain, warning and scaffold arms.
